extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, and creative writers interested in poetic and narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of critical maxims and practical guidelines about poetic diction, blank verse, imagination vs fancy, editorial practice for older texts, and qualities of prose and travel writing. Useful for writers, editors, and critics evaluating or producing literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakspeare's intellectual action
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare's intellectual action is wholly unlike that of Ben Jonson or Beaumont and Fletcher. The latter see the totality of a sentence or passage, and then project it entire. Shakspeare goes on creating, and evolving B. out of A., and C. out of B., and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat great dramatic writing as emergent and process-driven rather than wholly pre-planned; allow thought to be carried forward by the sentence and scene itself. The simile of a serpent making a fulcrum of its own body suggests an organic, self-propelling development of material rather than static projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic foundation: observation vs fancy (Crabbe vs Southey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crabbe's poems are founded on observation and real life -- Southey's on fancy and books. In facility they are equal, though Crabbe's English is not upon a level with Southey's. In Crabbe there is an absolute defect of the high imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetry, consider the source-material (real observation vs imaginative/bookish invention), the poet's facility of execution, the quality of diction, and the presence or absence of a 'high' imaginative power. Cultivate broad taste and weigh different strengths (accuracy of observation vs exquisite language) separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's sympathy with subject (Chaucer and Shakespeare)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sympathy of the poet with the subjects of his poetry is particularly remarkable in Shakspeare and Chaucer; but what the first effects by a strong act of imagination and mental metamorphosis, the last does without any effort, merely by the inborn kindly joyousness of his nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how naturally and convincingly the poet aligns feeling with subject matter: is sympathy produced through imaginative transformation or through an inherent tonal quality? The effect on readers (delight, tenderness) is a measure of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accessibility for Chaucer
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a few plain rules be given for sounding the final è of syllables, and for expressing the termination of such words as ocëan, and natiön, &c. as dissyllables,--or let the syllables to be sounded in such cases be marked by a competent metrist. Strike out those words which are now obsolete, and I will venture to say that I will replace every one of them by words still in use out of Chaucer himself, or Gower his disciple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical editorial steps to restore an older poet's popularity: provide pronunciation aids, mark syllables, and where appropriate remove or replace obsolete words (preferably with synonyms from the same older authors) while preserving significant historic terms. Do not over-modernize; retain meaningful archaisms when desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of voice and sentence construction (Shakespeare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare is of no age. His language is entirely his own, and the younger dramatists imitated him. The construction of Shakspeare's sentences, whether in verse or prose, is the necessary and homogeneous vehicle of his peculiar manner of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess style by how sentence construction embodies a writer's thought-logic; originality of voice can make a work 'of no age.' Strong writers use syntactic choices (sentence shape, rhythm) as instruments of thought and character, not mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank verse as a creative invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare's blank verse is an absolutely new creation. Ben Jonson's blank verse is very masterly and individual, and perhaps Massinger's is even still nobler. In Beaumont and Fletcher it is constantly slipping into lyricisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging dramatic or poetic blank verse, attend to how the meter serves thought and dramatic purpose; distinguish innovations from derivations and be wary of lyric intrusions that weaken dramatic blank verse. Compare across authors to identify different idioms of blank verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial method for corrupted drama (Beaumont and Fletcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: As for editing Beaumont and Fletcher, the task would be one immensi laboris. The confusion is now so great, the errors so enormous, that the editor must use a boldness quite unallowable in any other case. I can point out well enough where something has been lost, and that something so and so was probably in the original; but the law of Shakspeare's thought and verse is such, that I feel convinced that not only could I detect the spurious, but supply the genuine, word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors working with heavily corrupted or composite texts must sometimes act boldly, conjecturing lost words and passages guided by an understanding of the author's 'law' of thought and verse. Such bold emendation is exceptional and should be justified by intimate stylistic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper basis for literary comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a miserable mode of comparison which does not rest on difference of kind. It proceeds of envy and malice and detraction to say that A. is higher than B., unless you show that they are in pari materia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare authors and works only on like-for-like grounds (same genre, aims, or materials); avoid rank-ordering unlike works without establishing common criteria. Good comparative criticism should establish shared terms of comparison before pronouncing superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in travel writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Lewis's 'Jamaica Journal' is delightful; it is almost the only unaffected book of travels or touring I have read of late years. You have the man himself, and not an inconsiderable man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value travel writing that presents the genuine person of the author rather than artifice. Authentic voice, unsentimental observation, and a sense of the writer as present and engaged are marks of successful travel prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must suit language: blank verse prosody
rubrics_metrics.description: The trochaic termination of German words renders blank verse in that language almost impracticable. We have it in our dramatic hendecasyllable; but then we have a power of interweaving the iambic close ad libitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metrical forms compatible with a language's natural word-stress patterns. What works metrically in one language may be impossible or ungainly in another; account for prosodic tendencies when adapting forms across languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fancy vs Imagination (distinct faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fancy brings together images which have no connection natural or moral, but are yoked together by the poet by means of some accidental coincidence. The Imagination modifies images, and gives unity to variety; it sees all things in one. There is the epic imagination (perfection in Milton) and the dramatic (Shakspeare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative writing distinguish mere juxtaposition of striking images (fancy) from the higher power that unifies and transforms disparate material (imagination). Aim for imagination to give unity and meaning; beware that unchecked fancy becomes mere delirium, while imagination creates integrated vision (epic: distance/backward unity; dramatic: bringing elements together).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration's effect on narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Peter Wilkins is to my mind a work of uncommon beauty; and yet Stothard's illustrations have added beauties to it. If it were not for a certain tendency to affectation, scarcely any praise could be too high for Stothard's designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good illustrations can enhance and add to a text's pleasures, but they must avoid affectation; visual accompaniment should complement the narrative's tone and not distract or gratuitously embellish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of composition and wholesome tone (Fielding)
rubrics_metrics.description: What a master of composition Fielding was!... I think the Oedipus Tyrannus, the Alchemist, and Tom Jones the three most perfect plots ever planned. And how charming, how wholesome, Fielding always is! To take him up after Richardson, is like emerging from a sick room heated by stoves, into an open lawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novels and dramas by the solidity of plot design, the wholesomeness or corrective effect of tone, and the author's command of composition. Contrast plotting and tonal effects to judge reader experience (e.g., relief vs oppressive intensity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural authenticity for certain genres (desert-island fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe that Robinson Crusoe and Peter Wilkins could only have been written by islanders. No continentalist could have conceived either tale. It would require a very peculiar genius to add another tale, ejusdem generis, to Robinson Crusoe and Peter Wilkins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a work's conception depends on culturally specific sensibilities; for some genres or settings, authors whose lived experience resonates with the setting may produce uniquely convincing work. Authentic origin can be a criterion when assessing plausibility and tone.
